status: Six root-approved replacements integrated into existing land episode slots; six candidates remain unadmitted. No aggregate media wiring or publication.

characters.bio: A red panda who has found the perfect sleeping branch and would like the sun to stop moving.
A short-beaked echidna whose nose keeps making commitments her shoulders cannot honor.

entries.subject: short-beaked echidna
entries.title: From underneath
entries.body: I'm soft once you get to know me. You'll have to get to know me from underneath.

replacement.oldBody: Tried to turn around between two roots. There was room for one end of me or the other. After a long pause I backed out, bringing enough loose bark to imply I had been digging.

image.sceneMatch: Side view shows dense protective spines and the soft face and lower body; the intimacy joke depends on this contrast.

entries.payoff: Softness is available, but only from the anatomically inconvenient direction.

entries.subject: short-beaked echidna
entries.title: The wrong end
entries.body: A fly landed on the end of my nose. I waited for it to finish looking around. It was taking a very personal interest in somewhere I could barely see.

replacement.oldBody: A heavy footstep. I dug down and presented my spines. It passed. When I came up, I was facing the opposite direction and had forgotten which ants I was after.

image.sceneMatch: Frontal echidna portrait centers its long snout and small lateral eyes. The remembered fly is not pictured; no prey capture or precise visual-field claim.

entries.payoff: An inquisitive nose receives an inspection it cannot easily return.

entries.subject: short-beaked echidna
entries.title: The first sharp bit
entries.body:
The first spine caught me in the belly. Just a tiny prick. I shifted him and went back to sleep.

Then he shifted himself.

I had carried an egg, then a soft little mouth with feet. I was not ready for the mouth to start bringing equipment.

I made him a place in the earth. Checked the walls with my nose. Pressed the floor. Went over it all again, though I knew perfectly well what dirt felt like.

When I put him down, he curled against the warm place I had just left. A whole small echidna. I could see that now.

I stayed until he slept. Then a little longer.

When I finally lay down by myself, nothing poked me. I missed it. Not enough to put him back.

replacement.oldBody: A sneeze interrupted my tongue halfway into the log. Everything withdrew at once. Stood with my nose lifted, waiting for another sneeze, while the ants continued organizing themselves into a meal I was not having.

image.sceneMatch: Tasmanian echidna portrait shows fur and emerging-looking exposed spines. It illustrates the adult mother's remembered experience, not a pictured puggle or pouch.

entries.payoff: A mother misses the discomfort that signaled her child's growth, without wanting it back.

entries.subject: short-beaked echidna
entries.title: No teeth
entries.body: I have no teeth. I still wake from dreams in which they fall out. I would like to know whose worry this is.

replacement.oldBody: The old log split under my claws today. Inside it was soft, warm, busy, and nothing like the hard thing I had been walking around. I stuck my whole nose in and forgot to be impressed.

image.sceneMatch: Clear side profile centers the narrow beak; invented dream contrasts with actual adult toothlessness.

entries.subject: short-beaked echidna
entries.title: The black ground
entries.body:
The ground began roaring while I was halfway across it.

I put my claws down. Nothing gave. I lowered my head. The noise stopped, but something enormous was still there.

I waited. It waited.

There was grass only a little farther on. I could smell damp earth beneath it. I took one step toward that smell. Then another. Nobody touched me.

At the edge, my claws finally went into something. I dug until the noise came back and passed behind me.

Stayed there with my face in the earth for a while.

I had crossed an entire piece of ground that could not be dug. I couldn't stop thinking about what a terrible thing that was to make.

replacement.oldBody: Another echidna followed me around a stump. I stopped; he stopped. I reversed; he reversed. I finally climbed over a root. He went around it and was waiting, which felt unnecessarily competent.

image.sceneMatch: Actual echidna crossing a paved road, with reachable grass verge. Source photographer says they slowed after mutual panic; imagined inner account does not claim an impact.

provenance.title: File:Echidna on the road.jpg
provenance.creator: Petite Trotamundos
provenance.sourceDescription: As I was driving an echidna crossed the road. We both panic, I slowed down, the echidna stop walking... Then the echidna sort of waddled to the end of the road. Drive carefully!

entries.payoff: Pavement appears as ground stripped of the animal's main refuge, not as neutral infrastructure.

entries.subject: short-beaked echidna
entries.title: Occupied
entries.body: I pushed my nose into the gap beside the rock. Something touched it from inside. I withdrew. Waited. Tried again. It touched me again. Very well. Introductions were complete.

replacement.oldBody: Swam across the narrow creek because the other bank smelled interesting. Climbed out heavy and dripping. It smelled interesting from there too, but mostly like a wet echidna.

image.sceneMatch: Echidna probes a small actual gap among rock, bark and leaves. Unseen contact is fictional and not assigned a prey species.

entries.payoff: Repeated contact in the dark becomes an unplanned introduction.

entries.subject: red panda
entries.title: The hand underneath
entries.body:
Mother used to hold the bamboo while I ate. I would pull. She would hold. It was a very satisfactory arrangement.

One morning she let go.

The branch came with me. I fell backward with most of breakfast across my face. She waited until I had untangled myself, then put it between my paws.

I dropped it. She put it back. I tried to bite a leaf and dropped it again.

By the end I was furious with the branch and she had not finished her own meal.

The next day I could hold it. Not elegantly, but well enough to eat.

She reached underneath once to help. I let my paw loosen a little. Just enough for her to keep holding.

replacement.oldBody: Held a bamboo spray in one paw and picked out the tender leaves. Dropped the spray while rejecting a leaf. Ate the rejected leaf on my way down to collect the rest.

image.sceneMatch: Red panda grips bamboo in its paw. The present adult grip grounds a remembered lesson with its mother; no mother or cub is claimed in the photograph.

entries.payoff: The child can manage the branch but quietly prolongs a needed touch.

entries.subject: red panda
entries.title: Looking down
entries.body: I went to look at the ground. It was where I'd left it. So was the distance. Went back up with no useful news.

replacement.oldBody: The sun moved off my stomach. I shifted along the branch. It moved again. After three adjustments I was sleeping with my head lower than my feet, which apparently is what the sun wanted.

image.sceneMatch: Wild Singalila red panda points headfirst down a branch. It does not repeat the existing failed descent or claim a fall.

entries.payoff: The investigation establishes only that the familiar height remains high.

entries.subject: red panda
entries.title: A little
entries.body: I wasn't being rude. There was bamboo stuck to my tongue. I was being rude a little.

replacement.oldBody: Marked the low branch, then noticed another red panda watching from above. Finished very thoroughly. Had to walk past him afterward with the same bottom I had just made so much of.

image.sceneMatch: Close red panda portrait shows its tongue extended among bamboo leaves.

entries.payoff: The food excuse is true but incomplete.

entries.subject: red panda
entries.title: Nearly fierce
entries.body: I meant to growl. Yawned halfway through. He looked less afraid afterward. Frankly, so did I.

replacement.oldBody: Woke with my tail over my nose and an urgent feeling that somebody was too close. I pushed it away. Cold nose. Pulled it back. Whoever it was could stay.

image.sceneMatch: Red panda mouth open beside rocks and bamboo. The unseen observer and transition from growl to yawn are fiction, not a behavioral identification of this still frame.

entries.payoff: An attempted threat is interrupted by tiredness and becomes reassuring.

entries.subject: red panda
entries.title: Some assembly
entries.body: Someone has made a tree out of smaller trees and rope. I walked along it. Quite comfortable. I remain suspicious of how many trees were involved.

replacement.oldBody: Found a fallen berry and carried it up to my branch. It rolled off while I was arranging my paws. Watched it land beside the bamboo. Some meals are very determined to be bamboo.

image.sceneMatch: Red panda stands on an actual rope-and-stick climbing ladder. The artificial construction is acknowledged rather than disguised as wild habitat.

entries.payoff: A human climbing structure is assessed as an oddly assembled tree.

entries.subject: red panda
entries.title: The bad leaf
entries.body: There is a leaf in this mouthful I don't like. I don't know which one. I'm eating the lot out of spite.

replacement.oldBody: Somebody marked my tree while I was out. I sniffed the trunk, the fork, the low branch, the trunk again. By the time I finished being offended, I was late for my nap.

image.sceneMatch: Red panda portrait beside bamboo; it does not show a mouthful or a held bamboo bundle. Rejected for image and prose mismatch.

entries.payoff: Fussy selection turns into stubborn indiscriminate eating.
